content: The risk of contracting rabies can be significantly reduced by the prompt administration of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to individuals who may have been exposed to the virus. Research indicates that vaccinating 70% of the dog population is an effective strategy to prevent rabies outbreaks in at-risk communities. The success of such vaccination programs depends on understanding the ecology of the local dog population and the nature of human-dog interactions in the area. In developing countries, there is limited data on the incidence of human rabies. Estimates of human rabies mortality and the associated burden of disease, particularly in Africa and Asia, are often derived from animal bite injury rates and post-exposure vaccination rates. Rabies accounts for approximately 8 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) globally. However, with the rapid growth of dog populations and increasing cases of dog rabies in many countries, updated estimates are likely to show a significant rise in the disease burden. Children aged 5 to 15 years are at the highest risk of rabies due to their increased likelihood of being bitten and sustaining injuries in high-risk areas such as the head and neck. Mass dog vaccination programs initiated in Latin America in 1983 have achieved remarkable success. Human and canine rabies have been eliminated in Argentina, Chile, and major urban centers of other Latin American countries. Over 20 years of coordinated efforts by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) have led to a more than 90% reduction in dog-transmitted human rabies cases, although high-risk areas remain. For instance, rabies cases transmitted by vampire bats are increasing in some regions, attributed to environmental disturbances, migration, and limited access to healthcare in remote areas. The Alma Ata Declaration of 1978 emphasized the importance of community participation in healthcare planning and implementation. This approach has been instrumental in making health services accessible to the poorest populations in developing countries. For example, the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control (APOC), launched in 1995, established a sustainable community-directed system for distributing ivermectin to control river blindness. This program empowered communities to take responsibility for drug distribution and monitoring, saving an estimated 3 million DALYs between 1996 and 2005. It also provided indirect benefits such as improved overall health, deworming, better school attendance, and increased food production. Community-led Total Sanitation (CLTS) is another initiative that has significantly improved sanitation and hygiene in rural areas. This approach, pioneered in Bangladesh and now implemented in over 30 countries, encourages communities to analyze their sanitation practices and commit to eliminating open defecation. CLTS does not prescribe technologies or subsidize sanitation hardware but instead fosters collective action and behavior change. Communities achieving open defecation-free (ODF) status often experience improved hygiene practices, such as handwashing and protecting drinking water from contamination. Improved sanitation and hygiene are critical for reducing the transmission of zoonotic diseases, diarrheal infections, and soil-transmitted helminths. While systematic research on the impact of CLTS on zoonotic diseases is limited, cleaner environments are expected to lower infection rates. For example, better sanitation and restricting pigs' access to human feces are more sustainable strategies for controlling cysticercosis than relying solely on pig vaccination and treatment. Environmental interventions, such as CLTS, have demonstrated substantial effects on reducing diarrheal disease morbidity and mortality. These efforts also enhance human dignity and provide additional benefits, such as privacy and convenience for menstruating and pregnant women. CLTS has reached some of the poorest communities, enabling them to construct affordable toilets and improve hygiene practices. The approach has also inspired other community-led initiatives, such as improving food security and school attendance, particularly for girls. In summary, community-driven interventions like CLTS and APOC have proven effective in addressing public health challenges, particularly in resource-limited settings. These programs empower communities to take ownership of their health and sanitation, leading to sustainable improvements in health outcomes and quality of life.
